claims.text: A machine-learning-guided inverse-design approach can rapidly identify optimal refractory high-entropy alloy compositions.
Desired strength, ductility, and weight targets can be mapped back to compositional features.
The relevant starting design space is a broad set of multi-principal-element refractory alloys spanning many compositions.
A model trained on simulation and experimental data can predict RHEA performance metrics.
Inverse design can use model predictions to select promising RHEA compositions.
Predicted phase stability and microstructural features, including solid-solution phases and defect structures, mediate the balance among strength, ductility, and weight.
Training on high-dimensional data enables the ML model to capture complex correlations between composition and material properties.
Inverse design can pinpoint compositions satisfying specified property criteria.
Model-guided inverse design rapidly narrows the vast HEA composition search space.
The method will yield candidate RHEAs with superior or comparable mechanical properties relative to alloys developed using traditional methods.
The candidate RHEAs will have high strength and good ductility.
The candidate RHEAs will have reduced density relative to alloys developed using traditional thermo-kinetic and simulation techniques.
Traditional thermo-kinetic analysis and forward simulation require extensive exploratory iterations.
The approach's success depends on the comprehensiveness and quality of its training data.
The approach's success depends on the model's ability to capture nonlinear compositional effects in multicomponent systems.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits mechanical properties that are merely comparable to those of conventional alloys, whereas the falsification rule requires statistically significant improvements in strength and ductility. An outcome allowed by the prediction could therefore be classified as falsifying it.
